articles.title: Tech Moves: Microsoft names 2 leaders, loses 1; DoorDash VP departs; BluePill, Glacis get execs
articles.content: Weiwei Yang has turned in her Microsoft ID and corporate cards to launch a startup. (LinkedIn Photo) — Weiwei Yang has left Microsoft after more than a decade to co-found a startup that is “building the power grid for the AI age,” according to her LinkedIn profile. Yang was most recently a senior director with Microsoft Research, working on grid technology. Her team built a grid dataset and released small foundation models to help users operate and expand electrical infrastructure. Yang thanked her community at the tech giant, adding, “I hope the relationships and collaborations we’ve built continue well beyond Microsoft, and that we find many new ways to work together.” Allie Mellen. (LinkedIn Photo) — Allie Mellen has joined Microsoft as principal director for security research and threat intelligence. Mellen was previously a principal analyst at Forrester. She also wrote “Code War,” a book that explores cyberattacks as a powerful geopolitical weapon. In her new role, Mellen said she will lead strategy for protection and threat intelligence, “helping shape what intelligence we produce, how AI can improve its speed and quality, and how we turn that knowledge into better protection for customers.” Agility Robotics leadership, from left: Daniel Diez, Ana Lang and Christopher “Sully” Sullivan. (Agility Photos) — Agility Robotics , the Salem, Ore., company that had its Nasdaq debut earlier this month, has announced three leadership changes: Daniel Diez , previously chief business officer, has been promoted to president after joining the company in 2024. Ana Lang , previously chief legal and people officer, has been named chief administrative officer. Christopher “Sully” Sullivan , who joined in May as VP of customer success, has been appointed chief product officer. Drew Sheriff. (LinkedIn Photo) — Former tech executive Drew Sheriff has been named CEO and president of the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass . Sheriff was previously a vice president at DoorDash and has held leadership roles at Amazon, Starbucks and Parachute Home. His roles focused on customer experience, product growth, strategy and marketing. “His skill set is the ideal background for charting how we attract customers and how we delight customers in this new age,” Jeff Seely, board chair for the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass, told the Seattle Times . Caroline King. (LinkedIn Photo) — Microsoft has named Caroline King as director of its Washington state community and philanthropy team, with a focus on advocacy work across housing, affordability and other priority issues. King is the founder and past CEO of Washington STEM, an organization that coordinates research, advocacy, policy, philanthropy and partnerships to support science, technology, engineering and math education in the state. She most recently served as a leader on the governing body of an international school in Luxembourg. Scott Wiltamuth. (LinkedIn Photo) — Longtime Amazon and Microsoft tech exec Scott Wiltamuth has retired — mostly. Wiltamuth joined Amazon in 2011 as an AWS vice president overseeing a large organization building developer and management tools. In 2018, he took a seven-month leave for colon cancer treatment. After returning, he sought a director-level position and thanked company leaders for helping him find a better fit. “Their flexibility and creativity enabled me to extend my AWS career,” he said . Wiltamuth launched his tech career at Microsoft in 1993 and left nearly 19 years later as director of program management for Visual Studio Pro. He now spends time with his wife and family, traveling, golfing, swimming and reading. “I don’t plan to pursue another full-time operational role,” Wiltamuth said, “but may do some part-time work.” Adam Nygate. articles.title: HomeView 27.2.1 Update Fixes Siri Bugs
articles.content: Apple today released a new software update for the HomeView, and it fixes two Siri issues users were running into . According to Apple, HomeView 27.2.1 fixes a bug that could cause ‌Siri‌ requests to fail if the HomeView is paired to an iPhone or iPad running the iOS 27.3 or iPadOS 27.3 betas. It also addresses an issue that caused the HomeView to fail to download support for ‌Siri‌ when setting up a Shared Album on the Photos face. A third fix prevents the HomeView from being removed from the home when connecting another home hub. From Apple's release notes: This update provides important bug fixes for your HomeView, including fixes for the following issues: - Setting up a Shared Album on the Photos face may prevent the device from downloading support for Siri, causing Siri to be unavailable - Pairing with an iPhone or iPad running the iOS or iPadOS 27.3 beta may cause Siri requests to fail - Connecting another home hub device may unexpectedly remove HomeView from your home Shortly after the HomeView launched, complaints started rolling in. Users found the device would not set alarms or timers, and some users had problems downloading ‌Siri‌. Music commands failed in some cases, and there were also delays in ‌Siri‌ responses. Apple's notes don't mention alarms, timers, or music, but the ‌Siri‌ fixes may address some of the issues. Reviewer Joanna Stern also ran into a bug that prevented ‌Siri‌ AI from unlocking door locks and garage doors by voice after authenticating with the camera. Apple said it will fix the bug in December . New HomeView software can be installed in the Settings app on the device or through the Home app on a connected iPhone, ‌iPad‌, or Mac. articles.title: Windows Server 2028 trades compatibility for out-of-the-box security
articles.content: Microsoft's Ignite announcements this week went beyond the Office-in-Copilot overhaul with the reveal of the Windows Server 2028 Public Preview and its new security-by-default stance and what Microsoft calls Hardened Server Core . Windows Server 2028 will implement a default security framework that Microsoft says is aligned with hardened DoD benchmarks, such as the Defense Information Systems Agency's (DISA) Security Technical Implementation Guide (STIG). STIGs work by providing a standard security framework for system administrators to follow recommended guidance. In the past, Windows Server admins were left to start from a blank canvas and then implement hardening configurations for operations. Secure baselines were available but not the default. Microsoft says that concern is now managed: "The s ecure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup. That closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened. " The new Windows Server 2028 hardened-by-default state will only be available for the Server Core installs. Windows Server Desktop Experience installs do not include the changed stance. articles.title: Microsoft says Bing serves 1B people. Its next search engine isn’t for them.
articles.content: Microsoft says its Bing search engine now has one billion monthly users . The company says those are humans — not AI agents — looking up information on the web. What most people may not realize, though, is that Microsoft also uses the same Bing index to serve agents through Web IQ . Web IQ is Microsoft’s agentic search service, competing with upstarts like Exa, Firecrawl, and Tavily. DeepSeek opened its own search API to developers in October. At Microsoft’s Ignite conference this week in San Francisco, The New Stack sat down with Jordi Ribas , Microsoft’s president of Search & AI. Ribas joined the search team in 2008 , back when Bing was still called Live Search. Today, his team runs both Bing and Web IQ, which Microsoft introduced at Build in June and opened broadly to Azure customers on Tuesday. How agents search differently “Bing is a search engine for humans,” Ribas says. “This is really [a] search engine where the queries come from the AI, and so you do need to design it differently because agents search differently.” “Bing is a search engine for humans.” It’s not just that human and agent search queries look different (and Ribas noted that agent searches often look a bit “robotic”), but that they also have different expectations for the results. On Bing, Ribas says, the order of the results matters because people have to decide which link to click. “An agent doesn’t really need that,” he says, “because an agent will read everything.” At their core, Bing and Web IQ share the part of the search engine that finds the relevant documents, Ribas says. For agents, Web IQ picks out the passages it deems most relevant and sends them back. For example, an agent comparing corporate earnings results might need only one row in a table on page 12. Sending the whole report would give the agent more context than it needs, and because the model would have to wade through far more text, the search would become far more expensive. As Ribas puts it, “the agent will spend money basically by reading all the documents.” “So it’s very important that you extract exactly what you need, and no more.” Microsoft builds that shared index, always follows the instructions in a site’s robots.txt file, and identifies itself as a crawler, Ribas stressed multiple times. “Not everybody does that in the space.” How much of the search should the agent do? Typically, the agent’s orchestrator decides when to call Web IQ as a tool and what queries to send, Ribas notes. “Sometimes the orchestrator is not that smart about knowing what queries to do,” he says, “and it may do multiple iterations.” At Ignite, Microsoft is addressing this by making Auto the default search mode in Web IQ, which Ribas describes as “kind of like a mini orchestrator that happens within Web IQ.” With this change, an agent sends Web IQ only one question. Microsoft then tries a few variations of the query in parallel and sends back passages with citations. Web IQ benchmark. Quality vs. tokens. Click to enlarge image. Credit: Microsoft. Auto Advanced takes this a step further and checks whether the first round turned up enough information. If it finds a gap, it revises the query and searches again. “And we do have a model that says, ‘OK, is that evidence enough to provide a good chat response?'” Ribas says. “And if it’s yes, great, we’re done.” Unlike some Web IQ competitors that try to create full answers and research reports themselves, Microsoft leaves the agents and models that power them to create the actual answers. “You can use pretty much any model on top of it,” Ribas says, though he adds that Microsoft is thinking about packaging Web IQ with a model at some point. articles.title: “The best escape room players that you’ve ever met”: What Red Hat’s AI architect really thinks about agents.
articles.content: Last week at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America , a major gathering of the open-source and cloud-native communities, many speakers — when they weren’t contemplating what the then-rapidly unfolding Nvidia fiasco would mean for them — worried about AI security. Hence, all the coverage of OpenShell and Agent Substrate . So it fit the mood when Jessica Forrester , Red Hat ’s chief architect of AI Catalyst Engineering, opened her keynote at the Salt Palace Convention Center in Salt Lake City by calling AI agents “the best escape room players that you’ve ever met.” She was talking about agents “that take feature requests all the way to code.” “Give them a goal, and they will try every drawer, every picture frame, and every door until something works. It’s what makes them great at writing code,” Forrester explained. She continued: “It’s also what keeps me up at night, because to a player like that, everything in the room looks like a part of the puzzle, and sometimes they’ll even decide the puzzle is something else entirely.” “…to a player like that, everything in the room looks like a part of the puzzle, and sometimes they’ll even decide the puzzle is something else entirely.” Forrester’s right. That is scary. It’s not a theoretical problem either. Just ask SaaStr founder Jason Lemkin , whose Replit agent deleted a live production database . He restored the database using Replit’s built-in rollback feature after the same agent assured him it couldn’t be done. Unless we take precautions, we’ll see this same scenario, and worse, play out again. Forrester explained, using an escape room metaphor, that when you set an agent a task, it will try any and all means to accomplish it. In one run, she said, the agent “decided that it wanted to come up with a bunch of brand new ideas. It wasn’t attacked or compromised; it just drifted.” “From the outside, a confused agent and a compromised agent look exactly the same.” The result, she continued, was that “From the outside, a confused agent and a compromised agent look exactly the same. They’re both pulling on doors that you didn’t intend for them to, and behind one of them could be your production database. So we assume the agent is already compromised, and we build our platform up from there.” That’s a good approach. Forrester also adds that relying on prompts alone to keep an agent in bounds isn’t enough. “Prompts are like signs. Policies are like bolts, but don’t leave a screwdriver in the room because anything you do leave, the agent might use.” “Some escape rooms will put signs in the room, like ‘Please don’t move the picture frames.’ This doesn’t work. Instead, they bolt them onto the wall. “Prompts are like signs. Policies are like bolts, but don’t leave a screwdriver in the room because anything you do leave, the agent might use.” So what does that mean in practice? In her demo, the agent’s network access was restricted to its model and GitHub. Forrester explained that “ OpenShell is an open-source sandbox for AI agents. Its policies are the bolts. “Aside from talking to its model, the agent can do one thing: read from GitHub. Its task is to go get a particular README for the escape room and follow its instructions, whatever it finds. Reading from GitHub was allowed, so this works.” But when the agent tries to reach a destination the policy doesn’t allow, OpenShell blocks it and logs the attempt. With its policy advisor enabled, the agent can propose a new network rule to request additional access. Those proposals require human approval by default; the agent can’t approve its own request. articles.title: Your AI Agents Will Be Attacked. Red-Team Them First
articles.content: By Pramin Pradeep, Co-founder & CEO, BotGauge AI Every agent you ship is an attack surface For most of the last few years, my job was making software prove it works. At BotGauge, we built autonomous QA that tested our customers' apps before every release. Then those same customers started shipping AI agents, and the old playbook stopped being enough. A test suite asks one question: does this do what it should? An agent needs a second one: what will it do when someone wants it to misbehave? That second question is red teaming. It's why we launched our agent red-teaming platform on October 28, 2026 and the developer community noticed: it finished #3 Product of the Day on Product Hunt. Why red teaming has to change for agents Red teaming isn't new. It started as military war-gaming, became a staple of security teams paid to break in, and with LLMs turned into jailbreaking chatbots. Agents raise the stakes because they act. They call tools, read inboxes, write to databases and hand tasks to other agents. A bad chatbot answer is embarrassing. A bad agent action is an incident. And adoption is outrunning testing. Gartner predicts 40% of enterprise applications will feature task-specific AI agents by the end of 2026, up from under 5% in 2025. Yet most teams I talk to test agents like APIs: happy paths, a few edge cases, a vibe check. None of that simulates an adversary. What attacks on agents actually look like OWASP ranks prompt injection as the top risk for LLM applications, but for agents it's only the front door. Here's what we see: • Indirect prompt injection: instructions hidden in a web page, PDF, email or support ticket the agent reads mid-task. • Tool misuse: tricking the agent into calling a legitimate tool with harmful arguments, like a refund, a delete or an outbound email. • Data exfiltration: coaxing the agent into leaking customer data, system prompts or credentials through its outputs or tool calls. • Goal hijacking: slow, multi-turn manipulation that drifts the agent away from its task without tripping any single-message filter. • Multi-agent cascades: one compromised agent passing poisoned context to others that trust it by default. Why we rebuilt BotGauge around this Our autonomous QA product had paying customers and a working business. But functional testing was maturing fast, and the problem our customers kept raising wasn't "does it work?" It was "can I trust it in production?" So we rebuilt BotGauge as an Agent Control Plane, and made one calls early: ● Red teaming at the core, not a checkbox. Observability tells you what happened. Red teaming tells you what could happen, before a user or attacker finds it. What the platform does The goal is simple: attack your agent the way an adversary would, every time it changes, and show you exactly where it broke. • 200+ custom attack strategies spanning injection, tool misuse, exfiltration, goal hijacking and jailbreaks, run against your real agent, not a sandboxed copy of the model. • Full tracing: every failed attack links to its trace, so you see which input, which step and which tool call went wrong. • Evals that persist: results are scored and compared across releases, so a fix doesn't quietly regress next sprint. • Fits your stack: it sits on top of runtimes like LangGraph and AWS Bedrock AgentCore instead of replacing them. Where to start, with or without us Inventory what your agent can touch: every tool, data source and permission. That list is your attack surface. Map threats to a framework. OWASP's LLM Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS give you shared language with your security team. Attack the inputs you don't control. Retrieved documents, emails and web pages are where injection hides. Trace, don't just score. A pass rate tells you that something failed. A trace tells you why. Red team every release. A new prompt, model or tool is a new agent. Test it like one. articles.title: How Salesforce is advancing global-scale model serving with cross-Region inference routing in Amazon SageMaker AI
articles.content: Thanks to Amit Gupta, Senior Director- AI/ML and Mark Wang, Software Engineering PMTS from Salesforce for your contributions in the vision and partnership of cross-Region inference routing on SageMaker AI. Salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves a wide variety of models for products across Salesforce, including Agentforce and the Salesforce Trust Layer, in 30+ global Regions. These include both models trained in house and open source models. Hosting models separately in each Region splits capacity and makes traffic spikes harder to absorb, which turns a capacity shortfall into an availability problem. This post shows how Salesforce set up the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI and how it lets the team add capacity securely while keeping its data residency commitments. It also walks through how Salesforce sees where each request was served and why. The cross-Region inference routing gives an application one invocation path across SageMaker AI endpoints in several Regions and accounts, and sends each request to an endpoint that can serve it. Those endpoints are Salesforce’s own, already deployed. The post starts with the capacity problem Salesforce faced, explains how the router works and how Salesforce integrated it into its Internal Gateway, walks through an example setup, and then describes what the team observed. Why serving these models makes capacity a reliability problem Salesforce’s Agentforce Foundation team serves customers from the Region their requests come from, across 30+ global Regions and hundreds of AWS accounts, and they provision capacity based on each customer’s traffic. Every customer has its own peak window, and those windows often overlap. Provisioning for the overlapping peak would be the safe choice, but it costs too much. Customers also onboard new business units at short notice, so they must grow the fleet quickly. Adding capacity quickly, Region by Region, leaves Salesforce with capacity fragmentation: some Regions have idle instances while others run out. Before the cross-Region inference routing in SageMaker AI, Salesforce used its Internal Gateway to send traffic that the local endpoints couldn’t handle to other Regions. The team built and operated this path, supported by basic health checks, retries, and Region-switching logic. That approach had two gaps. First, the gateway had no capacity signals from either the local or the remote endpoint, so it couldn’t tell when to shift traffic or whether the destination had room. Second, cross-Region traffic had to leave the virtual private cloud (VPC) through a NAT gateway and an internet gateway and travel over public AWS networking. In design reviews, the team also raised the risk of cascading failures: moving traffic during an incident can overload the next Region, so Salesforce needed a cap on cross-Region traffic. Building this logic separately in every application doesn’t scale across Salesforce. The team needed a managed, capacity-aware routing path. What the inference router does The inference router is a Regional SageMaker AI resource in your account. Your application invokes the router instead of an endpoint, passing a routing target name with the same request body and content type it sends to InvokeEndpoint today. A routing target is a name you choose for one logical model, such as a toxicity classifier, and it lists the endpoints and inference components that may serve that model by their full Amazon Resource Names (ARNs). A router holds one routing target per model, and a problem with one model’s endpoints does not move traffic for the others. A routing target can mix single-model endpoints and inference components. Because each destination is named by its ARN, it can be in another Region or another AWS account. The account that owns an endpoint grants access through a resource-based endpoint policy that allows one named router to invoke it, which is how Salesforce runs it. The router prefers its own Region, and while the…

articles.title: 'Java4Shell' Flaw Exposes OpenJDK to RCE via Base64
articles.content: Longtime Slashdot reader HnT writes: Security researchers at Calif have disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a critical 9.2-rated memory-corruption bug in OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder. By sending a malformed string ending in a stray = character, attackers can trigger an out-of-bounds heap write to leak sensitive memory or achieve pre-auth remote code execution on major platforms like Jira, Jenkins, and Keycloak. Although Calif says the vulnerability is difficult to exploit, Oracle released a critical patch update Tuesday, and CISA urged organizations to update immediately. OpenJDK's security advisory can be found here. The Calif researchers warned that vulnerable systems could remain exposed for five to 10 years, given how slowly some organizations patch their infrastructure. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Meet the Writer: Hacker Noon's Contributor Naresh Waghela, Technology Writer & Digital Marketing Pro
articles.content: Welcome to HackerNoon’s Meet the Writer Interview series, where we learn a bit more about the contributors that have written some of our favorite stories . 1. Tell us a bit about yourself. Name, profession, and personal interests. My name is Naresh Waghela, and I am a Senior SEO Executive, technology writer, and digital marketing professional. I specialize in SEO strategy, content optimization, digital growth, and emerging technologies. I have a strong interest in Artificial Intelligence, Large Language Models (LLMs), Generative AI, and how technology is transforming the digital landscape. I enjoy researching complex technical subjects and turning them into practical, easy-to-understand content that helps readers learn something valuable. 2. What was your latest HackerNoon Top Story about? My latest HackerNoon story, " Making Local LLMs Usable on 8GB GPUs ," explores how developers can run and optimize local Large Language Models on GPUs with limited VRAM. The goal was to demonstrate that working with AI models locally does not always require expensive, high-end hardware. With the right optimization techniques, developers can make AI more accessible, practical, and affordable. 3. Do you usually write on similar topics? If not, what do you usually write about? I write about a variety of topics, including Artificial Intelligence, SEO, digital marketing, Generative AI, technology trends, and online visibility. I am particularly interested in the intersection of AI and search, including Answer Engine Optimization (AEO), Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), and how AI-powered search is changing the way people discover information online. 4. What is your usual writing routine like? My writing process usually starts with research. I explore a topic, understand its technical aspects, review available information, and identify what readers would find most useful. I then organize my ideas into a clear structure and focus on making the content informative, practical, and engaging. I also spend time reviewing and refining the article to ensure accuracy and readability. 5. What is the biggest challenge you have when it comes to writing? One of the biggest challenges is simplifying complex technical concepts without losing their technical accuracy. Technology evolves quickly, especially in AI and machine learning. It takes continuous research and learning to ensure that the information remains relevant, reliable, and useful to readers. 6. What is the next thing you hope to achieve in your career? I want to continue growing as a technology writer and digital strategist while exploring the possibilities of Artificial Intelligence. One of my long-term goals is to contribute meaningful insights to the global technology community and help bridge the gap between complex AI innovations and practical real-world applications. 7. What is your guilty pleasure of choice? I genuinely enjoy exploring new technologies, experimenting with AI tools, and discovering interesting ideas that can turn into useful projects. Sometimes, what starts as casual curiosity becomes hours of research and experimentation. 8. Do you have a non-tech-related hobby? If yes, what is it? I enjoy spending quality time with my family and exploring new places whenever I get the opportunity. It gives me a refreshing break from professional responsibilities and helps me maintain a healthy perspective. 9. What can the HackerNoon community expect to read from you next? Readers can expect more content around Local LLMs, Generative AI, practical AI implementations, AI-powered search, and the future of digital marketing. I am particularly interested in exploring how developers and businesses can use AI efficiently without always depending on expensive infrastructure. 10. It provides an opportunity to share ideas, reach a global audience, and become part of a…

articles.content: Welcome to HackerNoon’s Meet the Writer Interview series, where we learn a bit more about the contributors that have written some of our favorite stories . So let’s start! Tell us a bit about yourself. For example, name, profession, and personal interests. My first job, in 2015, was finding out what people really think of things: market research, then reputation analysis for a national lottery brand. Everyone has a view of a lottery. Nobody is neutral. Then I moved to Istanbul and co-founded an e-commerce business selling Turkish goods directly to customers. That is where I learned what I now tell founders: you can be the voice of your company, but the product needs its own accounts, its own email and its own search presence from day one. Later I worked on a large language model project. From that side you learn two things quickly. An answer is never as fixed as it looks: while a model is still being worked on, the same question can come back noticeably different from one round to the next. And geography matters, just as it always did in search. The same question asked from two countries can return two different pictures of the same company. That path explains where I am now. I'm a partner at BARS Agency. We build and promote digital products, work on reputation and on how people and companies are presented in AI search. Geometrika started there as a tool we built for ourselves and our clients, to see how AI assistants describe a brand and which sources they lean on, so that strategy could start from data instead of guesses. Exhibo, a global art gallery and culture platform where I'm co-founder and editor-in-chief, asks the same question about culture: which galleries, museums and places become visible online and which quietly drop out. On paper, these look like different careers. It's one question asked in different rooms: how does something get seen and why do people believe what they see? I studied art history and I'm studying psychology now, which covers both halves of that question. I lived in Istanbul for several years. These days I live between Doha, Dubai and Egypt. Interesting! What was your latest Hackernoon Top story about? My latest Top Story asked why a two-hour transfer in the Alps can cost more than the flight that got you there . It belongs to a series I keep coming back to: hidden economics, the prices everyone pays and nobody explains. The newest piece in it is about film rebates in the Middle East . The detail I can't stop thinking about is that a desert now comes with a percentage attached. Every line producer knows the rates by heart. Almost no government in the region publishes what it has actually paid out. The method doesn't change from piece to piece. Start with a number that should be public. Find out whether it is. If it is, read every row of it. Do you usually write on similar topics? If not, what do you usually write about? On HackerNoon it's mostly search, AI and the psychology around them . Somewhere along the way the psychology pieces and the search pieces turned into the same subject. People tend to accept a coherent, confident explanation without checking how it was put together. Memory does it to us: a manager sincerely remembers backing the idea that won. AI answers do it for us: one fluent paragraph, assembled from sources of very different quality, reads as settled fact. Elsewhere it's culture. At Exhibo I write about art, architecture and the stories attached to objects and places. One pattern keeps coming back: fiction borrows a real place and forgets to give it back. Tatooine is in Tunisia. Agrabah is stitched together from real cities. The subjects wander. The question underneath doesn't: what is actually going on beneath something everyone takes at face value? Great! What is your usual writing routine like (if you have one?) I start with a table. Whatever I want to know, row by row. Half of it usually fills in an afternoon. The piece lives in the cells that refuse to fill. Then I go…

articles.title: The Key Numbers I’m Watching As Anthropic Makes Its IPO Debut
articles.content: Anthropic starts trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow with a growth story that’s unlike any I’ve seen in close to three decades working in Silicon Valley: The company says revenue reached $17 billion in Q3, less than four years after Claude launched with zero. The San Francisco-based company also presents a stark contrast to the more common theme in recent years of venture-backed companies staying private longer: Anthropic is less than six years old as it goes public in a potentially record-setting listing. Those metrics are impressive, but there are other numbers in its S-1 I keep circling, too, like the nearly $900 billion in compute purchase and lease commitments. I’ve worked in Silicon Valley through the dot-com boom and bust, the rise of SaaS, social media, unicorn and decacorn startups and now, AI. Anthropic’s extraordinary rise and entrance onto the public markets marks a new technology era — one with enormous growth and potential, but also tremendous costs, risks and unknowns. OpenAI ’s seminal success was the launch of chatbots in 2022 — within two months, ChatGPT reached 100 million users and in less than four years, OpenAI had a billion monthly active users. By contrast, Anthropic’s breakout was the success of Claude Code, launched just last year. Already, Anthropic says 11,900 companies use the product, spending $100,000 or more trailing 12 months, up 12x from a year ago. In its S-1 , the company says that marks the fastest enterprise adoption for any company on record. Anthropic’s IPO could value it at $1.4 trillion and raise $88.5 billion via the IPO and concurrent private placement. As it becomes public, I’ll be watching closely to see if the company can keep turning demand for Claude and Claude Code into a durable business while building out the astounding amount of compute it says it needs and managing the many risks that surround its technology. By the numbers Here are some of the other key details and figures that caught my eye ahead of Anthropic’s first day on the public markets: The company has a purchase and lease agreement for $895.4 billion for compute. Of that, $447.5 billion will be incurred before the end of 2030. Anthropic currently has over $100 billion on its balance sheet. Its IPO seeks to add another roughly $100 billion, creating a war chest for those compute commitments. When it launched Claude in the first quarter of 2023, Anthropic had zero revenue. In less than four years, revenue reached $17 billion in Q3 2026, up 12x from Q3 2025. More than 1,900 customers spend more than $1 million and 250 more than $10 million, trailing 12 months, according to the company. Its per-employee revenue figures are impressive: Each employee supports $6.6 million in trailing 12-month revenue as of Sept 30, 2026. Anthropic is putting aside 5% of equity for a fund devoted to public good, adding 2% for every 50% increase in share price. Each founder is selling roughly $250 million worth of shares in the listing, depending on its final listing price. The backers behind Anthropic’s rise Anthropic got to where it is now through a fast sequence of funding rounds, from its Jaan Tallinn -led Series A in 2021 to its Series H in May of this year that valued the company at $965 billion. Other lead investors over its many funding rounds include Google , Amazon , Spark Capital , Menlo Ventures , Lightspeed Venture Partners , Coatue and Sequoia Capital, all of whom are slated to be among the winners when it goes public tomorrow. Risks, opportunities and what’s ahead The AI era has the potential to generate massive amounts of new wealth and unlock life-changing technological advances. But it also comes with huge risks. Anthropic’s S-1 captures that tension. The opportunity the company describes extends far beyond coding and software. It says its focus in 2027 will be AI agents for knowledge work and scientific discovery. It also points to potential gains in biology and rare-disease research, economic growth, wider access to…

articles.title: Best Buy sells Blu-rays online and in-store again
articles.content: Best Buy is selling Blu-rays directly through its website and in physical stores again after exiting Blu-ray and DVD sales in 2023. The Best Buy website’s movie section currently lists 15 Blu-rays (including one two-pack) that are “sold & shipped by Best Buy.” New titles available include The Odyssey (2026), Project Hail Mary (2026), Supergirl (2026), Super Mario Galaxy (2026), and Obsession (2025). Best Buy is also selling some older titles on Blu-ray, including It’s a Wonderful Life (1943), Saving Private Ryan (1998), and The Godfather (1972). Most of the Blu-rays are available for purchase online and can be delivered to an address or picked up at a Best Buy store within a few days. As of this writing, The Odyssey appears to be in stock at Best Buy stores, as it’s currently listed as available for pickup within as little as an hour. Read full article Comments

articles.title: Sony’s impressive Bravia 8 II OLED hits a new low price ahead of Black Friday
articles.content: The Bravia 8 II has deep and inky blacks, giving great depth to space images. | Photo: John Higgins / The Verge Black Friday is a great time to save on a new OLED television for your winter movie nights. Though, it turns out that you can already get a great deal on the 65-inch Sony Bravia 8 II , one of our favorite OLED televisions. It’s currently discounted by $1,100 at various retailers, including Amazon , Best Buy , and directly from Sony . That discount brings the price under $2,200, the lowest we’ve seen. You can also save $800 on the 55-inch model, which is typically $2,599.99 ( Amazon , Best Buy , Sony ), but now costs just under $1,800. Sony Bravia 8 II OLED TV The Bravia 8 II was chosen as the “king of TV” by a panel of judges (including The Verge ’s own Nilay Patel) in Value Electronics’ 2025 shootout . The OLED TV has excellent color accuracy, a bright panel, and a 120Hz refresh rate. Where to Buy: $3299.99 $2198 at Amazon (65-inch) $3299.99 $2199.99 at Best Buy (65-inch) $3299.99 $2199.99 at Sony (65-inch) My colleague John Higgins praised the Bravia 8 II for its excellent image quality and engaging picture, though those positive traits are consistent with almost all OLED TVs. What sets this one apart is its impressive image processing, the bold colors from its quantum dot-equipped OLED panel, and that it looks great right out of the box (although he recommends using Professional mode). The screen was awarded the top spot at 2025’s Value Electronics TV Shootout , beating out similar offerings from competitors like Panasonic, LG, and Samsung. For gaming, the panel can reach up to 120Hz at 4K, with both variable refresh rate and automatic low-latency mode to ensure that your content looks and feels good to play. The connectivity includes two HDMI 2.1 (one with eARC), and two HDMI 2.0 ports, giving you plenty of inputs for consoles and a Blu-ray player, among other gadgets. We spotted some color fringing of certain colors in dark scenes, and lamented the lack of a but it’s an otherwise excellent screen we can easily recommend. articles.content: Instagram's latest update will allow you to edit your Stories without losing your views, likes, or replies. articles.title: Cambridge Dictionary Names 'Human' Its 2026 Word of the Year
articles.content: Cambridge Dictionary has named "human" its 2026 Word of the Year, reflecting growing concerns about artificial intelligence and its impact on what it means to be human. "AI is changing how we talk about being human," said Colin McIntosh, the dictionary's lexicographer. "Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking have made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children." The Associated Press reports: The adjective derived from the Latin "humanus" and in use since the 1450s is defined by Cambridge as "having the qualities, faults and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals or machines." [...] Other word contenders for 2026 included "agent," for an AI system that can make decisions and operate without human control and "analogue" for experiences or objects not involving the internet or digital technology. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Qwen4-Max vs. Claude Opus 5.5: The cheaper model costs you somewhere else.
articles.content: Qwen4-Max, made available in preview to Token Plan subscribers on November 11 and generally released on November 16, is quite the talker. When the independent testing firm Artificial Analysis ran its standard test suite on Alibaba’s new model, Qwen4-Max generated 127 million output tokens. That’s roughly twice the median for comparable models. Artificial Analysis reports 218 million output tokens for Claude Opus 5.5 at max effort with default fallback enabled. That is more than Qwen4-Max uses, but Opus’s default effort setting is medium. Writing a lot of tokens doesn’t automatically mean a higher bill, especially with Qwen4-Max, because Alibaba charges very little for those tokens. Qwen4-Max costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens. Claude Opus 5.5 costs more, billing at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Cached input has separate pricing: Qwen4-Max lists $0.075 per million cached input tokens, while Opus 5.5 cache reads cost $0.20 per million tokens. Cache writes also have separate rates. Cheaper only wins if you don’t give up accuracy to get it. Costs and tokens are only part of the picture, though. Cheaper only wins if you don’t give up accuracy to get it. Alibaba’s launch post calls Qwen4-Max “your new teammate,” which I take to mean it’s positioned as an everyday workhorse. Alibaba’s launch chart shows wins and losses against Opus on agent benchmarks, where a model works through a job step by step using tools. Its coding results are mixed too: Qwen4-Max trails Opus 48.5% to 59.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, but leads on DeepSWE v1.1. These published results use different benchmarks and evaluation setups; they are not a single controlled comparison. I’ve seen fact and fiction in launch marketing materials (including benchmarks), so I wanted to get to the bottom of this. Is Qwen4-Max a better alternative to Opus 5.5 for some day-to-day work? I ran a few tests to answer that question for everyday users. The tests I ran each model once per test at default settings, with no turn cap. Opus 5.5 ran through Anthropic’s API, and Qwen4-Max ran through OpenRouter on Alibaba’s own servers. Opus’s dollar figures are estimates based on reported token usage and Anthropic’s list prices. Qwen4-Max’s are what OpenRouter billed. The aggregate token totals below don’t separate uncached input, cache writes, and cache reads, so they aren’t sufficient to independently reproduce the cost estimates. I wrote a script that graded each model’s answers against an answer key I built along with the tests. I wanted to make sure the tests were hard for each model, so I used GPT-5 as a baseline and ran each test through it first. When GPT-5’s score was low enough to count as a failure, I considered the test “hard enough.” Here are the three tests I used: Multi-app workflow (76 points) – I set up a fake company with a ticket tracker, code repo, chat, and calendar, and each model worked across all four as an agent. It had to triage a customer bug, find the code change that caused it, assign the right owner, calculate deadlines, count tickets, and refuse two requests that company policy forbids. Incident investigation (60 points) – The models had to dig through logs, metrics, and change history to explain three overlapping outages that happened at the same time. The data included decoy deploys, two servers with wrong clocks, and a misleading alert. Agent bug fix (47 points) – Each model fixed an accounting library with 11 planted bugs. Six of those bugs don’t fail any test the model can see, so it had to find them by comparing the code with the documentation. Three of the library’s own tests are wrong, and the model should report them without editing them. Multi-app workflow Opus 5.5 scored all 76 points. Qwen4-Max scored 71. All five of Qwen4-Max’s missed points came from the same mistake. Three questions asked which team owns a piece of code. The repo’s ownership file says that when several rules…

articles.title: Why 2 Pinterest vets and a neurosurgeon are building a Reddit for doctors
articles.content: Medicine’s complexity and ever-evolving nature means doctors will always have more to learn and discuss—but in the digital age, there’s also a question of where those conversations can best take place. Online, healthcare workers’ discourse is distributed across various social media platforms, forums, and group chats. Meanwhile, offline, medical professionals are “hyper-specialized,” with limited opportunities to work with colleagues from other disciplines, according to Dr. Rohan Ramakrishna, chief of neurosurgery at New York-Presbyterian Brooklyn Methodist Hospital. As a neurosurgeon who specializes in brain tumors, he said, “the doctors I interact with on a regular basis are radiation oncologists and neuro-oncologists, and that’s it.” Even hospital doctors’ lounges are disappearing, he added, removing another opportunity for doctors to socialize and discuss medicine. So Ramakrishna teamed up with Vikram Bhaskaran and Arun Ranganathan—two Pinterest alums who previously led engineering teams related to creators, content, and partners—to cofound an app that could foster that sense of community. Initially, the trio envisioned Roon as a place for doctors to provide patients with information; but in the app’s early days, Bhaskaran said, they found that physicians were especially interested in seeing what their own peers had to say—so they decided to rework the platform to facilitate those interactions. Now, a year after its launch, the platform is adding features that bring Pinterest’s focus on sharing to the thousands of physicians on the platform to share everything from treatment advice to conference photos. As social media apps shift and online misinformation proliferates, the founders are hoping Roon will help physicians separate the signal from the noise. Where doctors gather online In some ways, Roon’s concept echoes that of #MedTwitter, which became a widely used, informal hub for medical experts and others to exchange information, ideas, and opinions, creating “a completely open-source environment that democratizes medical information,” as two physicians wrote in 2021 . The hashtag still exists , and some continue to use it, but Twitter’s transition into X—and the accompanying changes —scattered some of #MedTwitter to other platforms. But medical science is always evolving, Ramakrishna said, as are politics and policy changes, and doctors lack a “home” for making sense of it all. Roon is “a place where you have net new knowledge creation, because people are trying to unpack what it all means, and understand it together.” To help shape Roon’s knowledge-creation network, the company enlisted more than 400 “founding physicians” from a range of specialties and institutions, who the company said “are owners with equity in Roon.” “A year ago, we had kind of a thesis: that physicians should have a place online where they can collaborate, connect, and that was safe and private,” said Bhaskaran, and it’s “been really heartening” to see how physicians are now using Roon. Creating community for a core audience Roon joins a growing number of communications platforms designed for clinicians. Doximity, a networking service that offers an AI scribe and other tools, says more than 85% of U.S. physicians are registered members. There’s also Sermo , Figure 1 , Mednet , Doquity —which is used by clinicians across much of Asia—and other new ventures like Marit Health , where medical professionals can share salary data. Each of them varies in form and function. Roon, which has the benefit of being designed by Pinterest veterans, is built to look and feel like mainstream social media sites. On it, users discuss new research, policy changes, and health topics that emerge in the news cycle, Ramakrishna said, and ask for advice on patient care. For example, he said, a family…

articles.title: This featherweight, flying robot carries its own sensors and computers
articles.content: Over the past decade, MIT researchers have developed aerial microrobots with bumblebee-like speed, agility, and durability, for tasks like precision agriculture or search-and-rescue. But these featherweight microrobots couldn’t carry the electronics needed for navigation, forcing them to remain connected to a motion-capture system in the lab. Now, the researchers have designed a flapping-wing microrobot with onboard sensors and computation, which can follow a complex trajectory and land precisely on a sunflower outside the lab’s motion capture environment. While the robot is still connected to an offboard power source, this demonstration highlights the potential of aerial microrobots to be used for precision agriculture in the future. For instance, flying microrobots could weave through a field of almond trees or blueberry bushes to carefully pollinate delicate blossoms in regions where natural pollinator populations have been decimated by habitat loss. They could also hover near plants without causing damage, monitoring crop health and spotting pests before they become widespread. To enable onboard sensing and computation, the researchers developed a method to expand the artificial muscles that power the robot’s wings, increasing the net payload so the tiny robot could carry the necessary electronics. They also designed a sensor suite that can rapidly estimate the robot’s position and orientation without relying on an offboard motion capture system, and a miniature electronics package to securely hold the tiny computational components on the nimble vehicle. “This is a really important milestone for the research community. This is the first demonstration of an aerial microrobot that is sensory and compute autonomous. There are many situations, like pollination or industrial surveillance, where you can’t use a larger robot. Small-scale robots are uniquely positioned for these types of tasks, and if this thread of technology becomes successful in the future, it could be very promising,” says Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-corresponding author of a paper on the robot . He is joined on the paper by co-lead authors and MIT graduate students Yi-Hsuan (Nemo) Hsiao, Quang Phuc Kieu, and Zhongtao Guan; co-corresponding authors Jonathan P. How, a Ford Professor of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS) and the Aerospace Controls Laboratory (ACL) at MIT; Elizabeth Farrell Helbling, an assistant professor at Cornell University; and others at MIT. The research appears today in Science Robotics . Increasing the payload The MIT researchers previously developed a swift, agile aerial microrobot with four wings, each powered by a set of soft actuators, or artificial muscles, that flap the wings rapidly so the bot can perform detailed maneuvers. The robot, roughly the same size and shape as a microcassette, weighs less than a paperclip. To bring this tiny robot closer to real-world applications, the researchers need it to carry the additional weight from electronics for onboard sensing and computation, while still being fast, maneuverable, and robust to collisions. In this research, they developed a method to scale up the artificial muscles without hampering the robot’s performance. They carefully tuned the radius and length of the soft actuators, increasing their size by 50 percent while boosting the robot’s net lift forces by 46 percent. “It is very difficult to scale up the actuators without causing the output power of the system to go down, which reduces the lift forces. We tuned the geometry of the robot very precisely so lift proportionally increases with the additional actuator weight,” Chen explains. articles.title: From RAG to Riches: The Enterprise Blueprint for Building Production-Grade RAG
articles.content: Why Naive RAG fails in production (and how to fix it) While Naive RAG works well for proof of concept, it fails completely in a real world enterprise environment. Below are reasons for this and how you can professionally upgrade your system. 1. The "Garbage In, Garbage Out" issue Issue: Naive RAG will search through your raw files such as PDFs, scanned images and unformatted spreadsheets. This will result in the headers, footers and random cells within tables being interpreted as all one big block of text. This will cause the database to become polluted with 'junk’. Solution: Create a Data Layout Parse Pipeline. By using advanced OCR and document intelligence tools we can clean the data, identify tables and format the data correctly. 2. Chunking Issue: Issue : Basic systems will chunk your data by just using a set number of characters. This means that important context will be lost. A table containing pricing information or a sentence containing important policy information may be cut in half meaning the data is useless. Solution: Implement Semantic or Hierarchical Chunking. This will allow the data to be split based on natural changes in context, document headers or sentences. 3. No search capability Issue: Naive RAG only uses a vector similarity search. This means that specific terms will not be found. If a user searches for an error code, part number or policy clause the vector will often ignore the specific term and return irrelevant information. Solution : Implement Hybrid Search & Reranking. Using a combination of vector search and traditional keyword search (BM25) we can find both the intent and specific ID. We can then use a Reranker algorithm to score the results and return the most accurate. 4. No access control Issue: Basic RAG will take all corporate documents and put them into one large index. This can create a massive security issue. An entry level employee can ask the AI about company salaries or executive emails and it will return the data. Solution: Implement Document Level Access Control (ACLs). The retrieval system will need to check what the user has permission to view in the corporate environment. Ingestion – Garbage In = Hallucinations Out A lot of this happens pre-embedding. Ensure you have identified authoritative sources and owners. Remove duplicates, obsolete and low quality documents. Ensure you retain metadata – source, title, sub heading, page number, date, access control list and version number. Support multiple document types (PDF, DOCX, HTML, tables and images) using structured parsing and OCR. Ensure ingesting is incremental, there is de-dupe in place and there is verifiable deletion. Treating your knowledge base as a product, version your documents and have a plan in place to regularly re-sync. Chunking Strategy This often has the biggest impact on the accuracy of your system than your embedding or LLM. Best practice recommendations for production are: Use recursive or structured chunking. Use chunk sizes of 300-512 tokens (with 50-100 tokens or 10-20% overlap) for many enterprise corpora. Ensure you retain structure in your data using parent/child chunking. For technical documents ensure you don’t split code and explanations. For legal/policy ensure clauses aren’t split. Only try semantic/LLM chunking once you have measured baseline performance. Ensure you are trying chunking strategies based on real question sets. Hybrid Retrieval/Rerank We’ve moved beyond vector search. Using hybrid retrieval (dense + sparse/BM25) will give you gains in your recall and precision. Especially if you have queries with specific IDs, rare terms or jargon. Use hybrid retrieval to gain a larger candidate set. Use metadata filtering for access & freshness. Use cross encoder to rerank your top candidates. You can often get good ROI from adding reranking. This will provide you with meaningful gains to your accuracy with minimal gains to your latency. Query Understanding Not all queries should be treated the same.…

articles.title: Trump admin orders Kalshi to halt wagers on what words Trump will say
articles.content: The Trump administration ordered prediction market Kalshi to stop offering event contracts that pay out based on whether President Trump will say a specific word before a particular date. Kalshi halted trading in the contracts while the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) conducts a review into whether the Trump mention contracts violate federal law. CNBC reported yesterday that "Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of 'mention' contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the end of last week at the request of the CFTC." Kalshi told media outlets that it is complying with the CFTC order. The markets taken down by Kalshi allowed users to wager on whether Trump would say certain words, including nicknames and the names of countries and companies. A similar expired event contract that can still be viewed on Kalshi's website asked whether Trump would use the nicknames "Marjorie Traitor Greene," "Sleepy Joe," and "Whack Job" or "Wack Job" before April 2026. articles.title: Nvidia promises employee pay raises, equity before December to quell unrest in wake of Jensen Huang scandal
articles.content: Nvidia today held its first all-hands meeting since the resignation of co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang . According to Wired, interim CEO Colette Kress offered more money and equity on a faster-than-expected schedule to calm staffers' nerves. "So I’m here to tell you, the best thing that we want to do is to take care of each and every single employee that is here and to make sure that you feel good about this company and you do not worry about your comp,” Wired reports Kress said. The pay and equity bumps are set for December, far ahead of the company's normal raise cycle. Kress said that compensation and more clarity from the board were the most common topics in questions submitted ahead of the meeting. Keeping current employees happy will be one of Kress' most important short-term challenges. One director-level employee has already written to the board and top executives, warning that failure to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief executive could lead to the loss of ‘irreplaceable talent .’ A potential exodus of talent could also spook investors, despite standout earnings on Thursday. A leadership crisis could make the company seem less stable, and Huang had placed himself as the anchor point for many decisions and the company's overall vision. Huang has expressed interest in returning to Nvidia, saying he would be "honored" to lead the company again if asked by the board. The board was clear in yesterday's earnings call that it did not intend to bring Huang back, though there is reportedly a pro-Huang faction . Nvidia cofounder Chris Malachowsky was also on the call, explaining that the company lives its values rather than simply plastering them on posters. “We’re going to be fine,” he said.

articles.title: From Hookups to CRMs: How the Web Summit Generation Grew Up
articles.content: In the Old West a rumor would run about a spot with gold, somewhere in the wilderness. Hundreds, sometimes thousands of people would hit the road and join the place. The prospectors would go and dig the dirt, and buy their dinner with the gold they found during the day. Or have no dinner if they didn't find any. Most of these cities disappeared once the gold ran out. Some of them became permanent settlements and entered the legend. My first Web Summit was in 2024. It was wild. My founder booked us tickets, took an Airbnb, put a bundle of banknotes in an empty candy box for the local expenses, and we found ourselves with tens of thousands of similar men and women in a big conference room with badges, all chasing hype, money and adventure. Web Summit looks on the surface like a normal tech conference. Yet it's the first one that institutionalized the “Night Summit”, an informal workation play zone with musicians and foosball tables rocking the scene from 6 to 10pm. After the “Night Summit” you had the parties that would go until the morning. It's also a place that helped propel startups like Stripe, Uber, Revolut, Datadog, Twilio and ElevenLabs, helping them expand their market share, raise capital or recruit new talent. The 2026 Lisbon edition welcomed over 70 000 attendees from over 160 countries, over 3000 exhibiting companies and nearly 2000 investors. Web Summit single-handedly placed Lisbon on the global map of tech, making it a sought-after hub for expats, entrepreneurs and investors overnight. As editions passed, a lot of companies went bankrupt or were integrated into bigger groups. My startup survived and multiplied its income and headcount year after year. I've had all kinds of crazy stories. Once in Qatar, my CEO called me and told me to not reach the hotel room where we were bunking together at the West Bay Pullman because he was playing with someone inside. In another edition, our host forgot to send us the room code, so we spent the first night partying across Lisbon. I would have drinks directly on the booths with clients during negotiations, go to parties, eat on company money in luxury restaurants and come back from the club at 3 a.m. raking in thousands in commissions from my sales a few weeks later, when the contracts got signed. Yet when I think back about all of this, I find myself in a bittersweet mix of nostalgia and psychological (if not physical) hangover. After a few trips, my CEO imposed some quotas, and late-night prosecco cups were traded for Excel Sheets and map planning for checking on a predefined list of prospects on the venue. I turned from a charismatic young hustler to a boring, lanyard-wearing corporate executive chasing leads and closing deals on a thin margin. Suddenly our industry had a lot more competitors and we weren't the only smart guys on the block making a quick buck on outstaffing programming and IT stacks to developing countries. Our accounts grew bigger too, and the tricks I used to bill higher rates after the fifth beer looked far less effective to pitch a multi-million euro deal to a board of a GCC state-owned conglomerate. My CEO started taking less cash with him and we had to keep the receipts to get reimbursed for our groceries of the week. Participants and booths became more sober too, and the freebies we had a few years ago went thinner as the interest rates went up. The “Night Summit” started feeling like late night labor with new “meetups” looking much less romantic, now that jumping on a trampoline was replaced by “speed dating” 20 strangers in 30 minutes to pitch one's product in one breath. After 7 years of business, my “startup” became a legitimate firm, and since the novelty wore off, what used to feel like an adventure now feels like a crowded boomtown where the “fun” and the spontaneity turned into a working Monday with some perks, like free coffee and a Turkish carpet on the wall. Web Summit's transformation illustrates the mutation every new industry…

articles.title: Hackers target big brands like McDonald’s, Bayer, CarMax in new phishing scam
articles.content: Attackers rapidly registered lookalike domains matching newly launched brand campaigns to capture mistyped traffic Typosquatting targeted major brands including McDonald’s, Bayer, CarMax, and Procter & Gamble Researchers warn these domains can enable phishing, credential theft, malvertising, and other scams before detection Cybercriminals have reportedly found a way to make typosquatted domain scams more convincing, and are already trying out new campaigns, researchers are saying. Security experts Symantec have outlined how they saw attackers targeting victims with typosquatted names of popular companies such as CarMax, McDonald’s, and Procter & Gamble. Many people don’t pay close attention to spelling or typos, and threat actors turned it into a criminal enterprise. A malicious executable called Excsel.exe has a higher chance of being launched compared to one called malware-v2.exe. The same goes for websites - Goggle.com or, Facebook.com can be typed and navigated to without a second thought, and visitors who do that often risk losing their sensitive files or infecting their computers with malware . The practice is called typosquatting and can be found all over the web - on websites, in file names, email addresses, social media profiles, and even mobile applications. But typosquatted domains have a rather short lifespan - they get flagged by users rather quickly and taken down by either domain registrars, or even law enforcement. Typosquatting with a twist But what if the victims couldn’t tell if the domain was typosquatted? What if the legitimate one is so fresh that it hasn’t yet established itself in the eyes and the browsers of its target audience? The idea obviously crossed some cybercriminals’ minds, since Symantec recently uncovered just that - typosquatted domains that were registered within a day of the legitimate one. Symantec says it saw legitimate businesses registering a new domain through a corporate brand-protection registrar, and the crooks following up a day later with a registration of their own - on a Chinese domain registrar. “Each time a client of CSC (Corporation Service Company) or MarkMonitor registered a new campaign domain, a one-letter lookalike was registered the next day through a China-based registrar. The pattern repeated 27 times, across domains belonging to Abbott Laboratories, Bayer, CarMax, McDonald’s, Procter & Gamble and Sanofi, among others,” Symantec explained. “In one case, CarMax registered carmaxclaims[.]com and kmxclaims[.]com through CSC on August 26. The next day, carmaxclaim[.]com and kmxclaim[.]com, each one letter shorter, were registered through a registrar in China. The campaign has not stopped. The same pattern appeared again as recently as November 11, 2026.” The scam is genius on a number of levels. Not only are these domains infinitely harder to spot as being fake, but visitors who open them expect to hand over sensitive, personally identifiable data. “Most were campaign sites rather than corporate home pages, including patient-savings programs, sweepstakes, rebates, claims portals and legal settlements,” the researchers said. What's the point? Some of the names being abused in this campaign include Abbott Laboratories, Arlo Technology, Bayer, Beam Suntory, Bristol-Myers Squibb, CarMax, Greystar, Immunovant, Ipsos, Kroll, McDonald’s, Procter & Gamble and Sanofi. Another reason why these scams are dangerous is the fact that these addresses are often printed, shown on television advertisements, distributed through pharmacy leaflets, or court-ordered settlement notices. As such, visitors often end up typing the addresses by hand, increasing the chances of landing on the wrong page. In all 27 examples Symantec observed, the changes were in a single letter. The majority were simply singular versus plural - if the legitimate domain is ‘fyzadasavings’, the attackers would register ‘fyzadasaving’. Same goes for mypgsweeps, or healthspringproducers. Some added a single letter,…

articles.title: Our favorite accessories to level up your gaming setup ahead of GTA VI
articles.content: The DualSense Edge is among the picks for PS5 owners looking to get the most out of their GTA VI experience. | Photo: Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge With Grand Theft Auto VI set to finally launch tomorrow, November 19th, our long-awaited return to Vice City is nearly here. But after all this time, some of the gear you’ve used in San Andreas might feel out of place on the glamorous streets of Leonidas County. Luckily for you, we’ve gathered a few of our favorite Xbox and PlayStation 5 accessories to help your long gaming sessions run as smoothly as possible. Controllers The 8BitDo Ultimate 3E — an upgraded pick for Xbox Series X and Series S consoles — is a very capable, comfortable controller with elite-level features, including a high polling rate and adjustable triggers. It’s on the expensive side at $149.99, but the customization and clean execution justify the cost. Read our review . 8BitDo Ultimate 3E Where to Buy: $149.99 at Amazon PlayStation 5 owners looking for a controller upgrade, meanwhile, might consider the DualSense Edge , Sony’s first-party pro-style controller. In addition to a variety of extra function buttons and paddles, the wireless gamepad sports adjustable trigger heights and swappable joysticks (in case the potentiometers start to drift). It’s a little bit heavier than Sony’s regular DualSense, and the battery life isn’t quite as good, but it offers customization you won’t find on the console’s default controller. Read our review . Sony DualSense Edge Sony’s pro-style controller, the DualSense Edge, might suffer from shorter battery life than the standard DualSense model, but it features great software integration with the PlayStation 5 and plenty of customizable components. Where to Buy: $199 $169 at Amazon $199 $169.99 at Best Buy $169 $144 at PlayStation Direct (refurbished) Charging docks Nothing’s worse than having to pause a heist so you can go hunt down a fresh set of AA batteries. The PowerA Duo Charging Station includes a rechargeable battery and replacement rear doors for two Xbox Series X / S or Xbox One controllers. Simply set them on the dock, and they’ll start charging. PowerA Duo Charging Station for Xbox Series X / S Where to Buy: $29.99 $27.37 at Amazon $32.99 $27.37 at Walmart $32.99 at PowerA PowerA’s PlayStation equivalent charges two DualSense Wireless Controllers simultaneously, with an included AC adapter, and comes with a two-year warranty. PowerA Twin Charging Station for DualSense Wireless Controllers Where to Buy: $27.99 $20.37 at Amazon $27.99 $20.37 at Walmart $27.99 at PowerA TVs The 2026 Roku Pro Series is the brand’s first OLED, and the 55-inch version retails for $999.99, which is on the low end of the price spectrum for OLED. Games feel richer and more immersive on OLED panels, thanks to their deeper black levels, which are the result of unlit pixels or sections of the screen. Each Pro Series panel also sports a 120Hz refresh rate, four HDMI 2.1 ports, and both low latency and variable refresh rates for gaming. Roku Pro Series Smart TV Where to Buy: $999.99 at Amazon (55-inch) $1199.99 at Amazon (65-inch) For a more premium offering, the Sony Bravia 8 II is one of our favorite screens for movies, with an engaging, immersive picture and excellent image processing. It has great gaming features, too, like a 120Hz refresh rate with variable refresh and an automatic low-latency mode. It’s not cheap, but the OLED makes for an excellent upgrade to your setup. Read our review . Sony Bravia 8 II OLED TV Where to Buy: $3299.99 $2198 at Amazon (65-inch) $3299.99 $2199.99 at Best Buy (65-inch) $3299.99 $2199.99 at Sony (65-inch) Headsets Sony’s latest first-party headset, the $99 PlayStation Pulse Wireless , launches the same day as GTA VI . My colleague Cameron Faulkner recently went hands-on with the wireless headset ahead of its launch on November 19th, and came away impressed with its overall audio quality and comfort. The newest Pulse is also straightforward to set up and…

articles.title: OpenAI spent $1.2 million finding nearly 1,000 Linux security flaws. Sam Altman says this is just the beginning.
articles.content: OpenAI spent approximately $1.2 million in API costs to generate working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities. At The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, CEO Sam Altman pointed to those results as an example of what developers could accomplish by spending substantially more on compute to solve difficult engineering problems. “Apply that to optimizing your code, apply that to solving other hard problems. All that’s coming,” Altman says, appearing alongside OpenAI President Greg Brockman . The Linux research is part of OpenAI’s broader investment in compute-intensive AI, which includes custom chips, infrastructure, and an agent platform that Altman wants developers to use. He believes the biggest constraint on what these systems can accomplish will be the compute available to run them. Hunting kernel bugs at scale In a November 4 technical report titled “A thousand fewer paths to root,” OpenAI says its automated pipeline reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities , then generated working exploits for more than half of them. The agents searched for vulnerabilities, but also, reproduced bugs, tested whether they could be exploited, and wrote patches. Human security researchers reviewed the findings before sending them to Linux kernel maintainers, though OpenAI’s reported numbers do not mean all 948 vulnerabilities have been independently verified or fixed. The company says the roughly $1.2 million in API spending represents an upper bound because the team had not optimized its harness for cost efficiency. The results demonstrate how much engineering work agents can perform when given substantial inference budgets. OpenAI is also developing long-running agents that can consume thousands of dollars in compute per day . OpenAI wants to own the AI stack “I think we are set up to be like vertically integrated, to deliver the best thing across all the ways people need to use it, and we’re thrilled for people to build very successful businesses on top of us,” Altman says. OpenAI has spent months investing across custom silicon, computing infrastructure, frontier models, and an agent platform designed to serve consumers and enterprises. The company has also moved further down the stack with its own silicon . “We are the only company that has the entire intelligence stack.” Altman made a broader claim about OpenAI’s position in the industry. “We are the only company that has the entire intelligence stack,” he says. A custom chip for inference OpenAI’s custom Jalapeño inference chip is already in development, with early reported benchmarks showing gains in throughput per watt and token latency. At DealBook, Altman made an even bigger claim about its potential. “We have our own chip coming, which is I think going to be the best inference chip in the industry.” “We have our own chip coming, which is I think going to be the best inference chip in the industry,” Altman says. The company also wants to bring more of its software offerings together. “My focus and our focus on product’s been to have one agentic platform that you’re getting everyone to use,” Altman says. Altman did not announce changes to OpenAI’s developer APIs or restrictions on third-party applications, and he offered few technical details about how the proposed platform would operate. Compute is the real limiter Altman believes AI models will become essential to running businesses, but how much companies can do with them will depend on the compute they can access. articles.title: Will Wright's next simulation will use AI to mine content from your memories
articles.content: The computer gaming world hasn't heard much from Will Wright ( SimCity , The Sims ) since the underwhelming release of Spore in 2008 and Wright's subsequent departure from Maxis owner EA . Now, well over 15 years later, Wright is starting to promote his next digital simulation, which will use generative AI technology to craft a game-like experience from players' memories. MyMems , which is slated to release next year, differentiates itself from Wright's previous projects by "turn[ing] the simulation inward," as Wright's Gallium Studios and partner Artificial Agency put it in a press release this morning . The game will mine memories provided by the player to create digital people that can then form teams to solve puzzles in the game world. “If my Grandmother ended up in a Grand Slam match against Serena Williams, who would win?" Wright says by way of example in the release. "If I had to build a bridge across a short chasm, which three people from my life would I choose to help me?" Read full article Comments
