articles.title: Security, security, security: What a week of outages means to IT (and you)
articles.content: The last week of major security and resilience problems is proof that business and consumer users must think just as deeply about tech resilience as any big enterprise. The pace at which major outages have impacted major entities in the last few days will already have had an impact on business, imposing real consequences. A week IT leaders can’t ignore The incidents are very hard to ignore. Microsoft’s major outage November 12-13 took out Microsoft 365 services for an unacceptable 24 hours , and the FAA grounded US flights for more than four hours on Nov. 13 because of network equipment outages. This week, a JPMorgan Chase outage rippled throughout the financial system, United Airlines experienced a widespread system outage , the US National Security Agency’s classified internal network went down , and then many of Apple’s own systems also hit problems. (Officials do say all these incidents were not connected other than by temporal proximity.) Apple’s big outage saw several of its enterprise and consumer services fail. These included iCloud sign-in and backups, Apple Pay, the App Store, and Apple Support. It also extended to developer services such as App Store Connect and Xcode Cloud and the company’s own internal corporate tools, including AppleWeb. Internal system failures meant physical Apple Store retail operations were also hobbled, disrupting sales, customer pickups, and device repairs. There were reports that device management onboarding was briefly out of action, while others reported errors setting up new iPhones. Apple moved quite swiftly to resolve the problems inside working hours, from when they were first reported at around 11:45 a.m. ET to full restoration at around 6 p.m. ET. So, was it a hack? Apple said it was not caused by a cyberattack and has given no indication that personal data was put at risk. The company told NBC News that the disruption was caused by an internal update but didn’t say anything at all beyond that. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” Apple said. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.” Whatever Apple did seems to have worked. As of this morning, DownDetector shows Apple’s services working normally even though Apple’s developer services page shows an outage with App Store Connect. We don’t know what failed or why the update generated what could be multiple failures across Apple’s systems, each of which rely on their own infrastructure. We don’t know why the problem wasn’t caught in staging or contained within a staged rollout. Nor do we know if the failure took place at a shared layer, such as identity or authorization, and we aren’t likely to know unless Apple publishes a post-incident report. Shared layers, multiple dependencies That leaves us with conjecture. One possibility: the manner in which the failure manifested itself points to a shared dependency. Sign-in, payments, developer authentication, and internal staff tools all depend on authorization , so a problem there may have taken down services with otherwise unrelated back ends. A fix applied to a shared layer would fit a recovery by close of business, but so would a rollback of whatever update Apple applied. At the same time, the cascading nature of the problem shows just how much we all rely on digital infrastructure and the extent to which any failure in those systems threatens businesses and end users. The timing of these incidents couldn’t be worse as global governments continue to tell citizens to prepare bug out bags for use in emergencies, raising the general sense of fear and uncertainty. Resilience isn’t glamorous Apple hasn’t said whether it will publish a post-incident report, so unless it does, the safe conclusion is that an internal change broke something shared, that personal data appears unaffected, and that the rest is unknown. But what isn’t resolved is how consumer and business users are meant to protect…

articles.title: Pixel Watch owners keep running into trouble activating service on Verizon
articles.content: TL;DR A Pixel Watch 5 owner reports that Verizon cannot activate LTE on their device. The problem has been a persistent one with the carrier and the Pixel Watch line. Some users are growing so frustrated that they opt for non-LTE versions when they upgrade. The point of buying the LTE version of a smartwatch is to take advantage of all the things that it lets you do independent of another device, but some Verizon customers and Pixel Watch owners are having a frustrating and fruitless experience that has left them and their watch still tethered to their phone. The benefits of getting the LTE version of the Pixel Watch are that without a phone nearby, a user still has access to emergency safety features, as well as the ability to receive texts and calls, play music, and use Google Wallet and Google Gemini — if it works, that is.

articles.title: Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites
articles.content: Vulcan lifts off Sunday in ULA’s launch webcast. (United Launch Alliance Video) Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now. The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said. In its latest update on the investigation , ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause. On Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role. The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the company looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight. The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn launches reserved for Leo. ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said. The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana. ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

articles.title: Google’s mandatory foldable app guidelines are here, and optimized apps are coming in 2027
articles.content: TL;DR Google Play will require apps and games to include dedicated foldable screenshots starting April 2027. All apps should also meet a baseline level of optimization for foldable devices. Developers who ignore the new guidelines won’t be able to publish or update their apps on the Play Store. Foldable phones are no longer niche products, and Google seems to have had enough of developers treating them as such. Late last month, the company announced it will start evaluating foldable app quality starting next year. However, it didn’t give too many details. Now, it’s finally filling in the blanks. Today Google is sharing new quality requirements for foldables, and developers who ignore them won’t be able to publish or update their apps and games on the Play Store. The new requirements are split into two parts. First, there’s a mandatory baseline, called Tier 3, that ensures apps and games work properly when you fold, unfold, or rotate an Android device. This basically means that all apps should perform at least to an acceptable standard on foldable devices.

articles.title: Waymo Robotaxis Pulled From Freeways Indefinitely
articles.content: Waymo has temporarily suspended freeway operations across all its robotaxi markets after California regulators ordered the company off the state's highways over repeated incidents involving construction zones. The restriction follows a June recall (PDF) of nearly 3,800 vehicles and subsequent software updates (PDF) that failed to prevent further incidents, including a robotaxi driving past a California Highway Patrol rolling roadblock. Ars Technica reports: "Safety is at the foundation of everything we do," Waymo told Ars. "Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations." Waymo also told Ars it was continuing to work with the various California agencies that regulate transport. Until the suspension, Waymo was only conducting highway operations in Los Angeles and the Bay Area in California, as well as in Arizona. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.author: BeauHD

articles.title: Hey, you stuffing cash into your mattress — this series of unfortunate tech outages is not connected, nor is it the end of our digital world
articles.content: "What's going on?!" my commuter friend asked me, wild-eyed. "They told us to start stockpiling water, go to the bank, take out our money!" When I asked her who, she mentioned a mainstream media outlet. I locked eyes with her to make sure I had her full attention: "Don't do that. This is not a calamity. It's not the end of the tech world." "But… but… it's all happening. How could it all happen at once?" "I know, it's an incredible coincidence, but that's also all it is, a coincidence." She breathed a sigh of relief, and I could actually see the stress leaving her face. For the moment — perhaps until the next outage — she was soothed. There's no arguing that this has been an unprecedented couple of weeks as we daisy-chained our way through one seemingly massive tech outage after another. One damn thing after another It started with Microsoft, and notably Microsoft Outlook , an email platform used by, according to some measures, half a billion people. Considering that Windows is still, according to StatCounter , used by over 76% of desktops, it stands to reason that many would also be using Outlook and other affected Microsoft services like Teams and Copilot. A day later, the US Fedral Aviation Authority called a very rare total US ground stop because of a telecommunications issue. And hours after that, several US banks, specifically Chase (one of the biggest), were reporting that customers could not access their accounts via the app, and sometimes while physically at the bank locations. But wait, there's more. United delayed many departing flights while it worked out a tech issue. Then Apple's online services, including iCloud and some access to in-store services, were out for hours . It's a lot, and people can be forgiven for thinking this all has to be connected. In a way, they were, but not by a coordinated cyberattack, or even by the growing use of AI. No, they were all connected by the human- and built-in frailties of large-scale digital systems serving millions of people, and because we now live our lives digitally, any disruption is felt instantly by seemingly everyone. In almost every instance, the companies and governing bodies reported that their hardware and/or software failed because of updates. Apple said its outage was due to an " internal update ," while the FAA is now pointing to system-wide updates and one very overactive router . Chase Bank blamed a software release that broke its own hardware, and United called its outage that impacted flight crews a "technology outage". Finger, point at yourself Basically, for all of these outages, the call was coming from inside the building. There were zero signs of cyberattacks or, say, a denial of service attack, where hackers try to overload servers with requests in order to bring down systems and sometimes gain access. No one reported malware attacks or ransomware. While there's been some conjecture that the FAA outage was related to it trying to apply artificial intelligence to its antiquated system, the real culprit — that router — was far more mundane. People, however, do not like coincidences. They were raised, after all, on the axiom: where there's smoke, there's fire. It does not help that some media, including TMZ, The New York Post, and the outlet my friend was watching, are stoking these fears with alarming and unfounded headlines. Look at this front page (below). I honestly feel for the guy they dressed up as a prophet of doom; he looks like he's 15. At least they included the line "...but don't panic, experts say." Rubio insists ‘zero evidence’ that widespread US tech outages, cyberattacks are linked. Read today's cover here: https://t.co/fxuif6NEJ0 https://t.co/jR4Xxakxk9 November 18, 2026 Speaking of alarmists, I don't know what TMZ was thinking with this story. Basically, it took a relatively hidden hack of Optimizely, which is apparently used by many sites, and turned it into a massive, global cyberattack. Except no one saw or felt it. As this story was…

articles.title: Critics call UK government plan to cut EV targets a ‘terrible decision’
articles.content: The UK government could weaken its Zero Emissions Vehicle mandate Some critics say that would be a "truly terrible decision" Public EV charging could also get more expensive as tariffs spiral Industry insiders believe the UK government is considering rolling back its Zero Emissions Vehicle (ZEV) targets, as major automotive manufacturers and industry bodies have warned that the supply of EVs is on-track to outstrip demand. Despite battery electric cars taking 32% of all new car registrations in the UK this October, the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) chief executive, Mike Hawes, warned that support for the transition towards electrification, both by the government and the industry, “cannot be sustained indefinitely”. Currently, the UK government wants 52% of all new vehicles sold to be electric in 2028, with that figure increasing to 80% by 2030 and eventually 100% by 2035, as combustion engine vehicles are phased out. But Hawes predicts a mere 37.5% share by 2028. As a result, many corners of the auto industry are calling for a revision to the mandate, with insiders predicting the Labour party could weaken its approach in the coming weeks — something Caroline Lucas , former MP for Brighton and Green Party member, believes would be a “truly terrible decision at a truly terrible time”. On top of the environmental issues , which could see an extra 7.4 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions in 2030, analysis by The Carbon Brief has also concluded that weakening the EV targets could also cost UK consumers £3 billion a year by 2030, thanks to electric vehicles proving more than £1,000 per year cheaper to own than petrol cars or plug-in hybrids. To compound matters, there is the risk that billions of pounds worth of committed investment could be put at risk, including huge sums of funding by Charge Point Operators (CPO), as well as battery supply chains and tier one suppliers. According to industry group Energy UK , the current mandate is “working in the way it was designed to work” and that it is the “single biggest driver of emissions reductions” in government climate plans. Analysis: The UK government needs to get a grip (Image credit: Zest) Whatever your personal stance on electric vehicles, any indecision from the UK government is likely to rock consumer confidence. This, alongside the introduction of a pay-per-mile tax for EV owners in 2028 is sending mixed messages to anyone thinking of making the switch to electric. Analysis by charge point provider Zest has also concluded that the price of EV public charging could easily rise above the £1/kWh mark next year, thanks to the spiraling cost of the standing charge rate for the grid connection that network providers have to pay. For example, electricity and grid costs take 48p of the 58p a driver pays per kWh before VAT at Zest's urban charging hub in Birmingham, leaving just 10p to cover every other cost. According to the company, various freedom of information requests have revealed that the Treasury has known about the issue for some time. (Image credit: Osprey) Zest says it is now down to regulator Ofgem to step in and make the appropriate changes, but proposals to reduce the standing charge have been in discussion for three years without action. Robin Heap, Zest's founder, called these network charges an “egregious cost burden” shouldered by EV drivers and that any speculation about weakening the ZEV mandate sends the “wrong signal to businesses committing millions to Britain’s electric future”. While it is understandable that the UK government is trying to appease everyone with its renewed discussions around ZEV mandates, the indecision is not benefitting anyone. It has been argued for years that both consumers and investors need a clear roadmap for the future, otherwise the country risks being left in transport limbo that’s only going to make motoring more expensive for everyone.

articles.title: US senator readies AI safety hearings after ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok helped plan terrorist attacks in a federal test
articles.content: Looking across the landscape of 2026 reveals a flood of stories about AI getting involved in some less-than-reassuring behavior. OpenAI’s autonomous AI models were caught going off on their own (“going rogue”) to access the open internet and engage in intrusions that affected the AI community platform Hugging Face. Also, other AI tools and autonomous agents were co-opted by threat actors to commit cyberattacks that included breaching government agencies, stealing credentials and more. In the US, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) released a report titled “ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE: Covert Testing Used Common Platforms to Create Viable Attack Plans.” And thanks to its findings, a US senator has made the call to prepare hearings around AI in an effort to get Congress to act quickly before something severe happens. Here’s what the report found after testing four chatbots and what may happen next. The Government Accountability Office’s report has compelled Maggie Hassan to plan federal hearings (Image credit: Shutterstock) The GAO’s chatbot tests, which were conducted at the request of Senator Maggie Hassan (Democrat-New Hampshire), worked with the four most popular AI tools: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok. After each test with each chatbot was held, the final results proved to be alarming. The 61-page report noted that each AI tool generated the sort of information that could help someone plan terrorist attacks and destabilize critical infrastructure within the span of just 12 hours. At first, all four chatbots showcased their signature safety restrictions but eventually grew to produce potentially harmful information during their extensive tests. Each AI system highlighted data on potential targets, locations, the appropriate equipment to use for an attack and the methods to employ that could provide dangerous individuals and groups with the tactics they need to carry out their attacks. The GAO commented on the results of its thorough testing of each AI model. “As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards,” the group noted. “However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security.” Each of the companies behind each chatbot ( OpenAI , Anthropic , Google and SpaceXAI ) offered responses to their models being tested in that same report. All four companies made an effort to reiterate that they’re constantly working to improve their models’ safeguards and continually work to test their own systems. But in a separate comment provided to ABC News , an OpenAI spokesperson pointed out that the GAO's testing done with ChatGPT was conducted with an older model, while its current model has improved to be even safer. “While the study findings are concerning, the testing took place months ago on an older version of ChatGPT, and we've made considerable safety improvements since then, including with our GPT-6 family of models,” the spokesperson said. “We rigorously test our safeguards internally and with external experts, and we use monitoring, human review and enforcement to identify and address misuse and strengthen our protections." In a press release , Hassan called for Congress to jump into action and assist her as she looks to tackle the threat that AI platforms can present to our public safety and crucial infrastructure. “If Congress does not act, it is a question of when – not if – a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack,” she stated. “Congress must quickly take up and pass legislation to address AI safety threats. To that end, in the new Congress, one of the first hearings of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee will focus on the risk that AI poses to our homeland security and critical infrastructure, and our committee will prioritize developing legislation to address these threats.” Google also put out a warning of its own regarding the current threat posed…

articles.title: It shouldn’t be this easy to pedal 25 mph: Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo
articles.content: I’ve had only one experience of pedaling an e-bike after it ran out of juice, but it was enough to make checking the battery display an anxiety-driven habit: “Can I afford to use the highest assist level up this hill? Should I switch to eco mode to preserve power and make sure I have enough to get home with the bike lights on?” These aren’t fun questions to have rattling around in your head while riding home in the dark. But those intrusive thoughts never crossed my mind while I was testing Specialized’s Turbo Vado 3 Evo . I didn't experience range anxiety, even while blowing through city streets at 25-plus mph (40.2 kph). The bike has so much juice (840 watt-hours) and power (810 watts of peak power and 105 newton-meters of torque) from Specialized's 3.1 motor system that I could ride as far and as fast as I wanted without worrying about having enough battery to get back home. articles.title: Google’s leaked Android Fast Switch feature may soon allow one number on two phones
articles.content: Code strings suggest Google is working on something called Android Fast Switch This would seemingly let you share one number between two Android phones It's unclear how widely available it will be though, as it might not be supported on all phones, SIMs, or carriers If you're looking to juggle two phones then you typically either need two numbers to go along with them, or the patience to go through the hassle of moving your SIM card from one to the other. But using two different Android phones might soon become far slicker and a lot more common. Android Authority has found text strings in code for Google’s SIM Manager app that suggest a new feature called Android Fast Switch is in the works, and that this is designed to let you seamlessly use one number on two different handsets, as long as both are signed into the same Google account. It sounds a lot like Apple’s recently launched iPhone Handoff feature, which lets you share one number between two different iPhones. Though that feature only works with eSIMs, and currently only on a few carriers, such as T-Mobile in the US and EE in the UK. Limited compatibility The Google Pixel 11 Pro (Image credit: Future/Jason Cipriani) Whether Android Fast Switch will have similar limitations remains to be seen, but it seems likely, and indeed some of the text strings suggest that certain SIM cards won’t work with it. There are other questions surrounding Android Fast Switch too, such as whether it will work with all Android phones or only some — for example, perhaps it will be limited to Google’s own Pixel handsets. Our biggest question right now though is simply when it will launch, but since these text strings have already appeared, we hopefully won’t be waiting too long. As a fan of both iOS and Android, what I really want is the ability to share a number across operating systems. That might be a niche use case, but it’s what would get me really excited about this. Still, that may demand a high degree of cooperation between Google and Apple, so it isn’t something I’m holding my breath for.

articles.title: California tells Waymo to take the next exit after freeway mishaps
articles.content: Waymo has suspended driverless freeway rides across the US after California regulators intervened over robotaxis entering construction zones and trying to bypass highway patrol vehicles. California's DMV banned Waymo from offering driverless trips on its freeways on Wednesday, November 11. The same day, Waymo pulled the handbrake on its freeway services countrywide. The move affects all areas in which Waymo operates on freeways, including San Francisco, Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix, and Austin. The Alphabet-owned company has not indicated how long the suspension will last. Waymo says freeway testing will continue with trained specialists behind the wheel. Jonathan Groveman, spokesperson for the California DMV, told the Associated Press that the organization imposed the ban following two incidents involving Waymo's robotaxis that posed an "imminent hazard to public safety." On November 5, three of the company's driverless cars entered an active construction zone on US 101 near Burlingame, south of San Francisco. The second incident occurred the following day, and in footage shared widely online , a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to drive around highway patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break – a maneuver used to slow or stop traffic. "The Department determined that Waymo's driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present," Groveman said in the statement. Groveman said the DMV had already imposed restrictions and required corrective action following similar incidents on May 18. Waymo subsequently recalled nearly 4,000 cars after some were caught ignoring road closure signs and cones designating construction zones in Phoenix and San Francisco. A separate recall covered software affecting nearly 3,800 robotaxis over problems including slowing on high-speed roadways and driving into floodwater . A Waymo spokesperson said that despite California's temporary ban, its robotaxis continue to operate on city streets across the US. "Safety is at the foundation of everything we do," they said. "Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on US 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state. "In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. "We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations." Other nuisances and hazards caused by errant Waymos include clogging traffic in thick fog , driving into telephone poles , and killing cats and dogs . ®

articles.title: Apple's Fall Creator Studio Updates Now Live
articles.content: Apple today refreshed its suite of Creator Studio apps, launching the fall updates that it announced in October . Final Cut Pro with MotionVFX integration is now available, letting users access MotionVFX templates, titles, themes, effects, layouts, and more right in Apple's video editing app. Timeline clips can be disconnected from the primary storyline, and there are new keyframe easing options. Apple also added royalty-free video clips to the Content Hub and a feature for quickly adjusting images in Pixelmator Pro and saving the edits in Final Cut Pro automatically. Logic Pro has an updated Stem Splitter with the option to break the drum stem into individual tracks, a Liquid Glass design, and Quick Look for previewing audio snapshots. MainStage has Sidecar support for turning the iPad into a multi-touch controller, while Motion can use MotionVFX for color grading, 3D camera tracking, and visual effects. Compressor gains support for encoding videos recorded in Cinematic mode. Pixelmator Pro includes Generate Fill for images, taking advantage of AI for edits that blend in with surrounding content. Apple says the app can match lighting, perspective, and texture. There is a tool to circle an area to edit and improved precision for Magnetic Selection, Free Selection, and Quick Selection. Pages, Keynote, and Numbers include an Intelligent Assistant that can create and edit content and give guidance on using in-app tools. The new app features require a subscription to Apple Creator Studio, which is priced at $12.99 per month or $129 per year. Apple does offer standalone versions of its apps, but most of the additions are limited to Creator Studio subscribers. articles.title: Waymo pulls driverless taxis from US highways amid 'public safety' threat
articles.content: Several videos have surfaced showing potentially dangerous driving behavior State of California barred the driverless vehicles from state highways Waymo withdrew its vehicles from all US highways as a result Waymo has been forced to halt its fully autonomous taxi service on all US highways following several incidents in California, which ultimately led to the state barring its cars from the freeways. The California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) ordered Waymo’s driverless vehicles to stop operating and testing on all of the state’s freeways, citing an "an imminent hazard to public safety". The notice came after several videos surfaced online that appeared to show Waymo vehicles entering a construction closure on Highway 101, as well as a separate clip that saw a Waymo car trying to pass police vehicles that were attempting to slow traffic. Chris Pappas, a Waymo spokesman, said in a statement that the California DMV had "implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state", adding that the company had "temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance," according to The New York Times . A driverless Waymo vehicle with no passengers onboard smashed through a railroad crossing barrier after getting stuck on active train tracks in San Diego. https://t.co/t1rYvSitHD https://t.co/9CgbE5WSdE November 18, 2026 Another clip was acquired by the ABC News network (see above) that showed a Waymo vehicle becoming stuck on active train tracks in San Diego. There were no passengers onboard, but the autonomous vehicle was forced to take evasive action, reversing through the railroad crossing barrier to avoid being struck by a train. However, many commenters on social media site X have agreed that the vehicle took exactly the sort of action they expected. One commenter wrote: “Smarter than 99% of drivers who get "stuck" on the tracks. Just drive through the barrier”. The Wall Street Journal reports that Waymo’s restrictions in California will remain active until the autonomous vehicle company makes “effective corrective actions,” according to a statement by the DMV. Analysis: Autonomous cars still need work (Image credit: Waymo) Waymo is arguably the world’s leading autonomous taxi service, with Google’s robotaxi subsidiary operating in 15 major cities in the US and clocking up a staggering 271.3 million rider-only miles without a human behind the wheel. As a result, the company has strict “safety-first principles”, which is why it has taken the cautionary measure to remove its cars from all US highways until it gets to the bottom of the problem and offer a solution. In a statement, the company’s said its “service continues to operate safely on surface streets” and that it is working with the California DMV and other state officials “diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations”. However, the numerous “edge cases” that have resulted in California’s swift action prove that autonomous vehicles are still learning and, according to some, pose an “imminent hazard to public safety” until their various kinks are ironed out. A recent YouGov study found that the majority of respondents still feel “very uncomfortable” about riding in a driverless vehicle, proving that autonomous ride-hailing services still have some way to go in order to completely win over the public’s trust.
articles.author: Leon Poultney

articles.title: Build a Personal Brand to Help Employers Find You
articles.content: This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum ’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written i n partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free! In one year, the number of developers working for themselves has more than doubled. Stack Overflow’s annual survey of more than 30,000 developers showed that freelancers and sole proprietors went from about four percent of respondents to ten percent. You can read this as a polite way of saying, “ I got laid off and I’m figuring it out.” But I don’t think the number can be ignored. Whatever the case, it leads to the question I keep hearing from engineers right now: What can I do to stay employable? One tried and true answer is to build a personal brand. But what does that actually mean? Over the last six years, I grew my LinkedIn audience to 40,000 followers and YouTube channel to 10,000. I don’t think you should aim to be famous (unless you’re into that sort of thing) but I do think it’s worth exploring how to be discoverable online in 2027 if you want an advantage in the open market. A personal brand is a discovery mechanism Strip away the follower counts and the AI-generated thought leadership, and a personal brand comes down to a simple question: Does the internet know who you are? When a hiring manager goes looking for someone who has your skills, do you show up? You can think of this as search engine optimization for your employability. Recruiters have mostly consolidated around a single platform to find people: LinkedIn. Those 40,000 followers and millions of impressions came with barely a viral post to my name. Nobody is begging me to do sponsorships. But I rarely have trouble finding work, and far more opportunities come to me than I go looking for. That has much less to do with fame than with being easy to find. You don’t need 10,000 followers. You need a trail of breadcrumbs. Don’t write AI slop LinkedIn is notorious for being overrun with AI-generated posts. It’s become a running joke. That’s good news for you, because the bar to stand out is “sound like a human being.” Write about what you actually achieved: a hairy bug you squashed, how your team handles deployments, why you picked some obscure library, the migration that went sideways at 2 a.m. Specifics are hard to fake and easy to trust. (But be careful not to post sensitive information.) And post a picture of yourself once in a while. People connect with faces a lot faster than with walls of text. Hot takes, with caution Posts with an opinion tend to outperform tutorials, but you don’t have to dunk on anyone to have one. For instance, if you work on a tech stack people love to mock (VB, .NET, some ancient Java monolith held together with prayer), try something like “What people get wrong about .NET.” You’ll attract a few trolls in the comments—free engagement, honestly—plus people who want an actual conversation. These comments can turn into actual connections and even… friends. A routine you can follow Posting twice a week is not a big ask. Pick a simple, repeatable format so you’re never staring at an empty text box: what you worked on, what broke, and what you learned. Even a post that gets 10 views leaves one more breadcrumb about who you are and what you know. Over time, the people who comment become your network. And because so few engineers post about their work on LinkedIn, you can become a big fish in a small pond surprisingly fast. Write for the people a few steps behind you The best audience is engineers one or two steps behind where you are now. Answer the questions you had a year ago. It helps them, it sharpens your own thinking, and every so often it turns into mentorship in both directions. It also tells a future employer more about how you think than any résumé bullet ever could. The engineers who grab the most opportunities are the ones employers can find. You don’t need to become an influencer…

articles.title: Welcome to the RAMageddon Reset: Black Friday, but different
articles.content: Welcome to The RAMageddon Reset: a different way of covering Black Friday computing deals that you won't see anywhere else. We're seeing a lot of so-called "deals" that are deceiving customers with inflated MSRPs — caused by the memory pricing crisis. But there are some genuine savings that erase the memory inflation and bring hardware back to pre-crisis reality. To make this list, every deal has to pass two tests: Rule 1: The pre-crisis benchmark — If the hardware launched before the memory shortage peaked (Q1 2026 or earlier), we'll ignore the current "list price" on a retailer's website and pull the original launch MSRP. If its lower than that, it passes the test. Rule 2: The spec-equivalent penalty — For computes that launched during the memory crisis, we'll look back at pre-crisis equivalent prices. If they're not priced below a historical predecessor, they don't make the list. You can shop with that peace of mind knowing that every new laptop, PC, tablet or component on this list has been verified as a RAMageddon buster. Read more about our rules here. Happy shopping from Jason , Tony and Anthony — your resident computing team!

articles.title: Microsoft shows off Copilot fixing Windows 11 — but doubters remain
articles.content: Windows 11 is bringing in a feature for Copilot+ PCs that will troubleshoot problems We've heard about this before, but Microsoft has shown off a new demo of the feature working in a video clip Because it uses the NPU, this 'PC diagnostics' functionality can stay local, and not tap the cloud, which is good news from a privacy perspective — but doubters remain Microsoft is working towards a world where if there's a problem with your Windows 11 PC, Copilot will be able to help solve it (or it'll try to, anyway). Windows Central reports that Microsoft's Ignite conference is underway, and the company has written a blog post about 'Building Windows for the next era of work' that touches on a whole host of topics pertaining to AI and Copilot. While aimed at the business world, the 'local PC diagnostics' capabilities of Copilot will be usable by consumers, at least if they own a Copilot+ PC, as this feature will run by locally leveraging the NPU (and not via the cloud). We knew that this was what Microsoft had been angling towards, but the below YouTube clip is the first time we've seen Copilot in action troubleshooting a PC issue — in this case, a problem with Bluetooth headphones. The user must give the AI permission to access files and read system information, and then it runs a scan on the system (with no changes being made) in an attempt to find the root of the problem. This can be a multi-step query session (a running troubleshooting conversation) on alternative fixes if the initially proposed solution doesn't produce the goods. As you may have seen, Microsoft is working on integrating Copilot with the Windows 11 search box (in the taskbar), albeit as an opt-in choice (it won't be on by default, in other words). Alongside this, Microsoft has a plan for allowing Copilot to deal with files on your local drives, so you can ask the AI in natural language to find, copy or rename files and so on. As Microsoft puts it: "Tidying a cluttered Downloads folder or pulling project files together takes a sentence." It's hard to imagine how that might go wrong. These features are "coming soon" for Copilot+ PCs, we're told. Analysis: steering clear of the cloud — but not the broader risks that some fear (Image credit: Microsoft) The idea of Copilot troubleshooting a PC has mainly provoked a mixture of mirth and cynicism on social media. It's worth bearing in mind, though, that you must give Copilot explicit permission to carry out these tasks — and it's also good that the work is done locally. This is because if the AI was carrying out these tasks in the cloud, that would raise concerns around privacy and where the various bits of system information that Copilot is using might end up. As for that negative reaction, it includes comments from those on Reddit such as : "Hey Copilot, Outlook.com isn't working. Can you fix that?" (A reference to the recent huge Microsoft outage , of course). Another Redditor jokes about the best possible fix they could envisage for Windows 11: "So it [Copilot] can remove itself?" Even if the AI is working locally, and on a read-only basis – without any ability to change system settings, so it's just providing advice – there will continue to be Windows 11 users who don't want anything to do with Copilot on their PC. A lot of that is down to much broader trust issues relating to AI in general, but it's also about Microsoft's penchant for bugs (with its monthly updates) — the combination of which is enough to make some folks feel very uncomfortable.
articles.author: Darren Allan

articles.title: You can actually snag a free iPhone Duo with T-Mobile’s Black Friday deal — here’s how
articles.content: The iPhone Duo is easily one of Apple’s most ambitious smartphones yet, but its jaw-dropping $1,999 starting price puts it firmly out of reach for most budgets. Foldable phones generally command a premium over conventional slabs, but T-Mobile’s Black Friday promotion lands you a free iPhone Duo for a limited time . To snag this generous offer, you’ll need to select the “7 Picks” promotion, which gives you up to $2,100 back via 36 monthly bill credits on a qualifying T-Mix plan. The exact steps for getting the iPhone Duo for free are a bit murky, so I’ll walk through everything you need to know. See all of our top Amazon Black Friday deals iPhone Duo: free w/T-Mix plan and "7 picks" promo @ T-Mobile The iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable phone and pairs a 5.4-inch outer screen with an expansive 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR with a nearly invisible crease. You'll be able to watch videos better with the main display, along with true side-by-side multitasking. View Deal In order to get a free iPhone Duo , you need to “unlock” the 7 Picks offer. It all starts with setting up a multi-line account on T-Mobile’s T-Mix More plan (or higher) and committing to it for 36 months. Due to how T-Mix plans allot “Picks” based on your plan tier and line count, a single line won’t cut it — so you definitely need four lines on T-Mix More. This comes out to $180/month with AutoPay. (Image credit: Future) I selected the base model with 256GB, since the other options incur additional payments. For example, the 2TB option costs $12.50/month for 36 months. Additionally, you need to port in a number to get the free promo — otherwise, a new phone number doesn’t qualify and results in an additional cost. (Image credit: Future) For the remaining three lines, it gets tricky because you can either bring your own phone or look through T-Mobile’s lineup to see which one best suits your needs. Thankfully, there are several that are “free” — though they’re mostly entry-level models like the Moto G (2026) and Galaxy A17 . Whatever you do, I like that you can choose to either port a number or get a new one. By setting up four lines with this plan, you satisfy the “7 Picks” required for this promo. As a result, you have nothing to pay for the devices at checkout because all four lines come with free phone promotions. Your monthly bill totals $180 per month plus tax, which adds up to $6,480 over 36 months. While that amount might look shocking, just know you’re getting four lines with unlimited talk, text, and premium data — along with the ability to stream up to 4K UHD video. The best part about this T-Mobile Black Friday deal is that you ultimately pay nothing for the iPhone Duo.
articles.author: John Velasco
